job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**S. 2817 (as amended Oct. 6, 2026) — loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems**

**Definitions (Sec. 2)**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "by a single vessel."** The 10,000-ton threshold is measured per vessel, so an operator can run a fleet of vessels each recovering 9,999 tons and never trigger the prohibition. The definition should aggregate across vessels, operators, affiliates, and license areas.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "per year."** The Act does not say calendar year, license year, or rolling 12-month period, so an operator can straddle a year boundary (e.g., 9,999 tons in December, 9,999 in January) and recover nearly 20,000 tons in a few weeks without a violation.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "metric tons" unspecified as wet or dry weight.** Nodules lose a large share of their mass on drying, so the same lift can be reported as over or under the threshold depending on the convention used; the Act gives NOAA no authority to pick one.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery . . . from the seabed."** It is unclear whether "recovery" occurs when nodules are collected on the seafloor, lifted through the riser, or landed on the surface vessel. An operator using a seafloor collector that is not itself a "vessel," with transfer to a separate carrier, can argue no single vessel "recovered" anything.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "seabed" and "mineral resources" undefined.** "Seabed" may or may not include subsoil (relevant to sulfide and crust deposits), and it does not distinguish the international Area from the U.S. outer continental shelf, creating an unresolved conflict with OCSLA and Interior's leasing authority.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "the Secretary" is never defined.** No section identifies which Secretary (Commerce, State, Interior) holds this authority, so the catch-all clause may be unenforceable as written.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — standardless, discretionary expansion of a criminal prohibition.** "Comparable risks" has no criteria, no rulemaking or notice-and-comment requirement, no publication requirement, and no judicial review provision. Because Sec. 5(b) attaches a 10-year felony to this definition, it invites void-for-vagueness, fair-notice, and nondelegation challenges, and nothing prevents a determination from being applied to conduct that predates it.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — sub-threshold mining is lawful by default.** Until a Secretary affirmatively acts (with no deadline), any operation under 10,000 tons per vessel per year is simply legal, so the "prohibition" functions as a cap.

9. **Sec. 2(2) — "U.S. person" is far too narrow.** It covers only citizens and corporations organized under State law. It omits LLCs, partnerships, LPs, trusts, federally chartered entities, entities organized in D.C. or territories, lawful permanent residents and U.S. nationals, and, critically, foreign subsidiaries controlled by U.S. companies. A company can reorganize as a Delaware LLC or a Nauru/Tonga-sponsored subsidiary and fall outside the Act entirely.

10. **Sec. 2(3) — "covered vessel" threshold and "equipped for."** Vessels at or under 5,000 gross tons are not covered at all, and "equipped for" is ambiguous for modular systems that can be removed before port calls or inspections. The definition is also never used in Sec. 3, so it governs only the registry, not the prohibition.

**Prohibition (Sec. 3)**

11. **Sec. 3(a) — no flag-state jurisdiction.** The Act reaches "persons in the United States" and "U.S. persons," but not U.S.-flagged vessels. A foreign LLC operating a U.S.-flagged vessel on the high seas violates nothing, and a U.S. citizen crew member is arguably liable while the owner is not.

12. **Sec. 3(a) — "engage in" undefined.** The Act does not reach financing, owning, chartering, insuring, contracting for, sponsoring, processing, transporting, or importing nodules, and contains no aiding-and-abetting or conspiracy provision. U.S. capital and U.S. processing facilities can support foreign-flagged, foreign-owned mining without restriction.

13. **Sec. 3(a) — "person" undefined.** The Dictionary Act (1 U.S.C. 1) likely fills the gap, but relying on it for a criminal statute invites argument that only natural persons were intended.

14. **Sec. 3(b) — grandfather clause is open-ended.** It exempts mining "under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment," with no cap on volume, no expiration, no limit on subsequent amendments, expansions, or renewals, and no requirement that the license be in good standing. Any current licensee can scale to full commercial production indefinitely.

15. **Sec. 3(b) — "exploration license" undefined.** It could mean a NOAA license under DSHMRA, an ISA exploration contract held by a foreign sponsor, or any foreign national authorization. If read broadly, every existing ISA contractor with a U.S. parent is grandfathered.

16. **Sec. 3(b) — pre-enactment rush.** Because the cutoff is "date of enactment," any license issued between now and signature qualifies, creating an incentive to obtain or expand licenses in the interim.

17. **Sec. 3(b) — internal inconsistency with DSHMRA.** Under DSHMRA, exploration licenses do not authorize commercial recovery; permits do. The exception therefore either exempts nothing (because mining cannot lawfully be "conducted under" an exploration license) or implicitly authorizes commercial mining under exploration licenses, and a court could read it either way.

18. **Sec. 3(c) — environmental assessment exception has no limits.** There is no definition, no volume cap, no requirement that assessment be the sole or primary purpose, no agency approval, and no reporting. Pilot and test mining at commercial scale can be characterized as "for the purpose of environmental assessment."

19. **Sec. 3 — no conforming amendments to DSHMRA.** The Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) is neither repealed nor amended, so NOAA remains statutorily obligated to process license and permit applications, and a permittee can argue the specific later-in-time permit authorizes conduct the general prohibition forbids.

20. **Sec. 3 — no exemption for scientific research or government activity.** Without a research carve-out, large-scale sampling by academic or federal vessels could fall under Sec. 2(1)(B), which invites overbreadth objections and gives opponents an easy "this bans science" argument.

**Registry (Sec. 4)**

21. **Sec. 4(a) — no deadline, no penalty.** The registration requirement has no compliance date, and Sec. 5 penalties attach only to violations of Sec. 3, so failure to register or report carries no consequence.

22. **Sec. 4(b) — reports are useless for enforcement.** Reports must describe "recovery activities" but need not state tonnage, depth, location, or vessel identity, which are the only facts that matter under Sec. 2(1)(A). "Certified" is not tied to 18 U.S.C. 1001 or penalty of perjury, and "operator" is undefined (owner vs. charterer vs. manager).

23. **Sec. 4 — no verification tools.** The Act grants no authority to board, inspect, audit, require AIS/position data, or share information with the Coast Guard or Justice Department.

**Penalties (Sec. 5)**

24. **Sec. 5(a) conflicts with Sec. 8.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the prohibition is not effective until 180 days after enactment, so no violation can occur in that window. The clause is either surplusage or an attempt at retroactive liability that will be challenged.

25. **Sec. 5(a) — "each day on which the violation occurs" cannot be computed.** The violation is defined by annual tonnage, so it is unclear whether the violation "occurs" on the day the 10,000-ton mark is crossed, every day of recovery after that, or every day of the year.

26. **Sec. 5 — no enforcement machinery.** The Act names no assessing agency, no procedure, no judicial review path, no statute of limitations, no injunctive relief, no vessel seizure or forfeiture, and no license revocation.

27. **Sec. 5(b) — "willfully" plus vague definitions.** Willfulness will be nearly impossible to prove where the key terms (year, wet/dry weight, recovery, comparable risk, environmental assessment) are undefined, and the statute depends on an undefined Secretary's discretionary determination.

**International Agreement (Sec. 6)**

28. **Sec. 6 — hortatory and ambiguous.** "Seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation, and it is unclear whether the 18-month deadline applies to beginning or completing negotiation. No reporting requirement to Congress and no consequence for inaction.

**Duration (Sec. 7)**

29. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b) — contradictory.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress acts by joint resolution; subsection (b) sunsets the entire Act at 10 years regardless. Operators can simply plan commercial production for year 11.

30. **Sec. 7(a) — the National Academies report is never commissioned.** No section directs, funds, or sets a deadline for the report, so the condition for lifting the prohibition may never be satisfiable, or may be satisfiable by any NAS report an operator can characterize as relevant.

31. **Sec. 7(a) — "joint resolution" requires presentment.** A joint resolution is ordinary legislation requiring the President's signature, so the provision adds nothing beyond Congress's existing power to repeal, while creating confusion about whether a simple repeal would also suffice.

32. **Sec. 7(b) — no savings clause.** When "this Act" ceases to have effect, the penalty provisions lapse too; absent a savings clause, pending enforcement actions and penalties for pre-sunset violations may be extinguished.

**General drafting gaps**

33. **No severability clause.** If Sec. 2(1)(B) or the Sec. 3(b) exception is struck, a court must decide what remains; a severability clause would foreclose the argument that the whole Act falls.

34. **No rulemaking authority, no appropriations, no agency designation.** No agency is directed to implement anything (beyond NOAA receiving registrations), which leaves the undefined "Secretary," the threshold-measurement questions, and the registry with no mechanism for resolution.

35. **Effective date vs. registry (Sec. 8).** The 180-day delay applies to the registry as well as the prohibition, so the government has no information on who is operating when the ban takes effect.

**Most consequential for an operator:** items 1, 9, 12, 14, 18, and 29. Together they mean a U.S.-parented company can keep mining through a foreign or LLC subsidiary, under an existing license, at any scale characterized as assessment, across multiple sub-threshold vessels, with no reach to its financing or processing, and with a hard end to the regime in 10 years.
